decisions.mark: explains that `skipSync: true` stops the single incoming reaction being treated as the post's complete set — without it every other reaction on the post would be deleted
decisions.detail: QUOTE: `skipSync: true` | add path (hardcoded) | `sanitizeReactions` returns early with `deleteReactions: []`, so the add event never deletes stale reactions for that post. Only the create set is computed. | WHY: The answer explains that skipSync on the add path prevents deletion of other reactions on the post (the sync-diff would otherwise delete local rows missing from the single-reaction payload). || QUOTE: `skipSync: true` | add path (hardcoded) | `sanitizeReactions` returns early with `deleteReactions: []`, so the add event never deletes stale reactions for that post. Only the create set is computed. | WHY: The answer explains that skipSync on the single-reaction add prevents deletion of the post's other local reactions (which full sync mode would delete as missing from the payload). || QUOTE: `skipSync: true` | add path (hardcoded) | `sanitizeReactions` returns early with `deleteReactions: []`, so the add event never deletes stale reactions for that post. decisions.mark: notes that both handlers swallow any error silently (empty catch), so a failed write leaves no trace
decisions.detail: QUOTE: Both websocket handlers swallow errors with an empty `catch`. That hides failures, and it conflicts with the project rule to log errors with context. A malformed payload or a DB error leaves no trace. | WHY: The answer states both handlers use an empty catch, hiding failures such as DB errors, so a failed write leaves no trace. || QUOTE: "Both websocket handlers swallow errors with an empty `catch`.
